<header>
  <div class="hero">
    <div>
      <p class="kicker">Security and availability review · aftereightsousse.tn · 26 October 2026</p>
      <h1>Anyone can send emails to your customers pretending to be you</h1>
      <p class="lead">Your domain publishes no DMARC record and your SPF ends in a
      soft fail, so nothing stops a stranger from sending emails to your customers
      that look like they came from your reservations address: a deposit request, a
      table confirmation, a link. Nothing tells you when it happens. The second
      point, a menu that no longer draws, is more visible but simpler to fix. Both
      can be closed today.</p>
    </div>
    <div>
      <label class="toggle tg-lang" for="lg">
        <span class="track" aria-hidden="true"></span>
        <span class="off">FR</span><span class="on">EN</span>
      </label>
      <label class="toggle tg-theme" for="dm">
        <span class="track" aria-hidden="true"></span>
        <span class="off">Light</span><span class="on">Dark</span>
      </label>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="chips">
    <span class="chip">static React on GitHub Pages</span>
    <span class="chip">2 of 6 need action</span>
    <span class="chip">tested 26 Oct 2026</span>
    <span class="chip">no exploitation attempted</span>
  </div>
</header>

<section>
  <h2>Your domain has no instruction to reject a forged sender</h2>
  <p class="lede">Your domain's SPF record ends in <span class="mono">~all</span>,
  which tells receiving servers "soft-fail", and there is no DMARC record at all.
  Neither one stops a forgery. Together they are an invitation.</p>

  <div class="grid">
    <div class="panel">
      <p class="kicker">Highest impact · affects every customer</p>
      <div class="prose">
        <p style="color:var(--ink-2);font-size:16px;margin:0">A message arriving
        from <span class="mono">reservations@aftereightsousse.tn</span> that lands
        in the inbox, passes a quick glance, and asks a customer to confirm a
        booking by paying a deposit to an account that is not yours. Without
        DMARC, the receiving server has no instruction to reject or quarantine it,
        and you get no reports telling you it happened.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="panel">
      <span class="fig">0</span>
      <span class="fig-label">DMARC records published,<br>queried 26 Oct 2026</span>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="rows" style="margin-top:var(--s5)">
    <div class="row"><span class="k">SPF, as published</span><span class="v">v=spf1 … ~all</span></div>
    <div class="row"><span class="k">DMARC at <span class="mono">_dmarc.aftereightsousse.tn</span></span><span class="v">none</span></div>
    <div class="row"><span class="k">DKIM, seven common selectors tried</span><span class="v">none found</span></div>
    <div class="row"><span class="k">Receiving servers told to reject forgeries</span><span class="v">no</span></div>
  </div>

  <p class="lede" style="margin-top:var(--s5);margin-bottom:0">A one-line DMARC
  record in monitor mode costs nothing and cannot break your mail, because at
  <span class="mono">p=none</span> it instructs nobody to block anything. It just
  starts sending you reports. Move to <span class="mono">p=quarantine</span> once
  those reports are clean, typically two to four weeks.</p>
</section>

<section>
  <h2>The menu is a spinner that never stops</h2>

  <div class="grid">
    <div class="panel">
      <p class="kicker">Probably known already · here is the mechanism</p>
      <p style="font:400 1.3rem/1.35 var(--serif);margin:0 0 var(--s3)">Every dish,
      every price, unreachable. The page is not broken — it is waiting.</p>
      <div class="prose">
        <p style="color:var(--ink-2);font-size:16px;margin:0">The site is a React
        app. It loads a single JSON file from a Heroku app, and only then draws the
        menu. That Heroku app answers <span class="mono">503</span>, so the request
        fails, and the code that draws the menu has no error branch. The spinner
        stays.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="panel">
      <span class="fig">503</span>
      <span class="fig-label">HTTP status from the backend,<br>measured 26 Oct 2026, 01:00</span>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="pair">
    <figure class="shot">
      <img src="data:image/webp;base64," alt="The After Eight landing page: a photograph of the restaurant interior with the heading The Right Place To Enjoy Food And Relax, and two buttons labelled Menu and Call Us">
      <figcaption><b>What works.</b> <span class="mono">/</span> — the landing
      route, which needs no data. Photograph, heading, two buttons. This is what
      the owner sees when they check the site.</figcaption>
    </figure>
    <figure class="shot">
      <img src="data:image/webp;base64," alt="The menu page: a blank white page with only a small green circular logo centred and no other content">
      <figcaption><b>What does not.</b> <span class="mono">/#/menu</span> — the
      route one click to the right. The green mark is the loading spinner
      <span class="mono">loader.89ba5735….png</span>, still spinning after six
      seconds. Nothing else ever renders.</figcaption>
    </figure>
  </div>
  <p class="src">Both captured 26 October 2026, 01:00 Africa/Tunis, in a clean
  browser profile at 1240×800, six seconds after load. The menu capture is
  unedited apart from cropping the empty margins.</p>

  <div class="note">
    <p style="margin:0"><strong>The landing page is fine.</strong> It is a separate
    route with no data dependency. That is also why the failure is easy to miss: the
    site looks healthy from the front door, and it sits one click behind it.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<section>
  <h2>Why the spinner, in one drawing</h2>
  <p class="lede">Four steps succeed and the fifth has nowhere to go. The missing
  arrow is the whole bug. Compare the two paths out of the backend call.</p>

  <figure class="dgm">

      <desc id="f1d_en">The browser loads static files from GitHub Pages, which return 200. The app then requests a JSON payload from the Heroku backend. If that request succeeds the menu renders. If it returns 503, as it does today, no handler exists, the data state stays null, and the loading spinner remains on screen indefinitely.</desc>

    <figcaption><b>The failure branch, and the branch that never existed.</b>
    <span class="mono">Home.js</span> renders the spinner when its <span class="mono">data</span>
    state is still <span class="mono">null</span>, and only a resolved promise
    ever sets it. Because <span class="mono">App.js</span> chains
    <span class="mono">.then()</span> with no <span class="mono">.catch()</span>, a
    503 leaves the state untouched rather than raising something visible.
    Read from the published source map, 26 Oct 2026.</figcaption>

    <ol class="key">
      <li><span class="kn">1</span><span class="kt"><b>browser</b> loads <span class="mono">/#/menu</span></span></li>
      <li><span class="kn">2</span><span class="kt"><b>GitHub Pages</b> serves the static files, 200 OK</span></li>
      <li><span class="kn">3</span><span class="kt"><b>Heroku backend</b> is asked for the menu JSON. Today it answers 503</span></li>
      <li><span class="kn">4</span><span class="kt">with data, the menu draws. Without it, the spinner stays forever</span></li>
    </ol>
  </figure>

  <div class="rows">
    <div class="row"><span class="k">Backend URL, from the shipped bundle</span><span class="v">floating-spire-33339-….herokuapp.com</span></div>
    <div class="row"><span class="k">Response to <span class="mono">GET /data</span>, 26 Oct 2026 00:52</span><span class="v">503</span></div>
    <div class="row"><span class="k">Same URL over HTTPS in a browser context</span><span class="v">Failed to fetch</span></div>
  </div>

  <div class="note">
    <p style="margin:0"><strong>Two ways out, and the cheap one is better.</strong>
    Restart the Heroku dyno and the menu returns in minutes, but it will fail the
    same way the next time the app sleeps or the free hours run out. Moving the
    menu JSON into the GitHub Pages repo as a static file removes the backend, the
    503, and the bill at once.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<section>
  <h2>All six, ranked by what they cost you</h2>
  <p class="lede">Severity here is business impact, not CVSS theatre. A forged
  email outranks a dead menu page: the menu costs you sales, the email can cost
  your customers money. The first damages your reputation as well as your takings.
  The schedule for fixing each one is in section 07; this column is severity
  only.</p>

<section>
  <h2>Two doors onto your domain are standing open</h2>
  <p class="lede">This is the finding that looks alarming and is the least urgent
  of the three. It matters for one specific reason: the address would be real, and
  the certificate would be valid.</p>

  <ol class="steps">
    <li><span><b>Your DNS still points two names at GitHub.</b> <span class="mono">mail.</span>
    and <span class="mono">ftp.aftereightsousse.tn</span> both resolve to
    <span class="mono">185.199.108.153</span>, a GitHub Pages address. Nothing of
    yours is hosted there.</span></li>
    <li><span><b>GitHub answers with its own placeholder.</b> Ask for either name
    and you get <span class="mono">Site not found · GitHub Pages</span> — proof
    that GitHub is listening, and that no repository claims that name.</span></li>
    <li><span><b>The ownership check was never done.</b> GitHub only refuses to
    host a stranger's page on your domain if you have published a
    <span class="mono">_github-pages-challenge-</span> TXT record proving you own
    it. There is no such record anywhere in your zone.</span></li>
    <li><span><b>So a stranger can claim it without touching anything of yours.</b>
    They point their own repository at <span class="mono">mail.aftereightsousse.tn</span>;
    GitHub sees DNS already pointing at it and begins serving. Your DNS is never
    modified. The page appears in minutes, on your domain, with a
    <span class="mono">CN=*.github.io</span> certificate that browsers accept.</span></li>
  </ol>

  <div class="note">
    <p style="margin:0"><strong>What it is worth, and what it is not.</strong> No
    password and no customer data are exposed — the site has no login and sets no
    cookies. The prize is your name: a link people already half-trust, saying the
    menu has moved and asking for a card number. That is why it ranks below the dead
    menu: it needs someone to notice you, and the menu needs nobody to notice
    anything.</p>
  </div>

  <p class="lede" style="margin-top:var(--s5);margin-bottom:0">The fix is to
  delete both DNS records, since nothing lives at either address. If they are
  needed later, re-add them together with the verification TXT record that
  protects every subdomain at once.</p>
</section>

<section>
  <h2>The three smaller ones</h2>

  <div class="rows">
    <div class="row"><span class="k"><b>Source map published.</b> <span class="mono">main.f3b18514.js.map</span>, 1.5 MB, serves your whole component tree verbatim</span><span class="v">200 OK</span></div>
    <div class="row"><span class="k"><b>axios 0.27.2</b>, an April 2022 release, superseded twice over</span><span class="v">2022</span></div>
    <div class="row"><span class="k"><b>No CSP, no <span class="mono">X-Frame-Options</span></b>. A third-party script could be framed or injected</span><span class="v">absent</span></div>
  </div>

  <p class="lede" style="margin-top:var(--s5)">None of these hands anyone your
  data. The source map is the notable one in the other direction: it is how I
  read every file on this page without touching your server. That is a fair
  trade for a brochure site and a bad habit for anything with a login behind it.
  If you leave it up, know that the backend URL and the full routing logic are
  public.</p>

  <div class="note">
    <p style="margin:0"><strong>The bare domain, for completeness.</strong>
    <span class="mono">https://aftereightsousse.tn</span> fails its certificate
    check, because only <span class="mono">www</span> has a matching one.
    Visiting <span class="mono">http://</span> works: it redirects to
    <span class="mono">https://www.</span> and everything is fine. So this bites
    only the visitor who types the bare domain and gets an https attempt first. Some will see a warning and leave.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<section>
  <h2>What I would do, in this order</h2>

  <div class="panel">
    <div class="rows">
      <div class="row"><span class="k">1 · Bring the menu back, permanently: serve the JSON from the same GitHub Pages repo and delete the Heroku dependency</span><span class="v">today</span></div>
      <div class="row"><span class="k">2 · Publish a DMARC record at <span class="mono">p=none</span> and read the first week of reports</span><span class="v">today</span></div>
      <div class="row"><span class="k">3 · Delete the <span class="mono">mail.</span> and <span class="mono">ftp.</span> A-records</span><span class="v">this month</span></div>
      <div class="row"><span class="k">4 · Turn off source map generation in the build, or accept it knowingly</span><span class="v">this month</span></div>
      <div class="row"><span class="k">5 · Upgrade axios, add a redirect from the bare domain, then tighten DMARC to quarantine</span><span class="v">this quarter</span></div>
      <div class="row"><span class="k">6 · Then, if the mood takes you: one page, a menu, no way to order. The site does its job; it does not do it well. We can talk about the rest.</span><span class="v">whenever</span></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <p class="lede" style="margin-top:var(--s5);margin-bottom:0">Steps 1 and 2 are
  both under an hour of work and neither needs a developer. Step 1 is the only one
  that changes a number you can see.</p>

  <p class="lede" style="margin-top:var(--s4);margin-bottom:0">The first five steps repair what is
  broken. The sixth is not a repair: the site is short, one page, no way to book
  online, and it was built to last an afternoon. It does its job. It is a front
  door, not yet a room.</p>
</section>

<footer>
  <p style="margin:0 0 var(--s3)"><b>How this was tested.</b> Passive review only,
  on 26 October 2026 between 00:45 and 01:05 Africa/Tunis. DNS queried directly;
  HTTP responses and headers read with curl; the application source read from the
  site's own published source map; the menu failure observed in a clean browser
  profile. No exploitation was attempted, no credentials were used, and no
  destructive test was run against the live site.</p>
  <p style="margin:0 0 var(--s3)"><b>What I did not verify.</b> That the subdomain
  claim in section 05 would actually succeed. I did not attempt it, because
  attempting it means taking control of content on someone else's domain. The
  reasoning is from GitHub's documented behaviour and OWASP's subdomain-takeover
  guide, not from a live attempt. Treat it as well-evidenced, not proven.</p>
